questions.question: At the top price, Matangi Rubber Limited's P/E is 16.6x. Similar listed companies have a P/E of about 27.7x. What does that tell you?

choices.text: It costs about the same as, or less than, similar companies for each rupee of profit.
It costs more than similar companies for each rupee of profit, so its profit must grow faster to be worth it.
The P/E shows how many shares the company has.

questions.explanation: A P/E of 16.6x against 27.7x means you pay no more for each rupee of Matangi Rubber Limited's profit than for its peers'. That is a fair starting point, not a guarantee.

numbers.name: peer_pe
numbers.label: Middle P/E of similar listed companies

questions.question: 20.8% of this IPO's money is an offer for sale. Where does that part of the money go?

choices.text: Into the company, to build new factories.
To the existing owners who are selling their shares.

questions.explanation: In an offer for sale, existing owners sell shares they already hold, so the money goes to them. Only the fresh issue, ₹99.10 crore here, reaches Matangi Rubber Limited.

numbers.name: ofs_share
numbers.label: Share of the IPO money going to sellers

questions.question: Sales went from ₹90.11 crore in FY24 to ₹129.76 crore in FY26, which is 20% a year. How would you describe that?
questions.explanation: 20% a year is healthy growth: Matangi Rubber Limited's customers are buying more each year.

questions.question: Matangi Rubber Limited owes 0.25 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0.25 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, Matangi Rubber Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.
